title: Educators Should Embrace the ‘Science of Math.’ Here’s Why h-heres-why/2026/10
author: Rick Hess
summary: Rick Hess interviews Daniel Ansari, a psychology and education professor at Western University who directs the Numerical Cognition Laboratory, about what a science of math is and is not. Ansari says it applies psychology, educational research and cognitive neuroscience to teaching and assessment, but the analogy to the science of reading is imperfect because math has no clear single learning sequence. He argues that both domains are cumulative, that fluency matters, and that instruction should be developmental because young learners are novices who benefit from explicit guidance and not from minimally guided discovery. Mastery of math facts frees working memory, with understanding of numerical symbols first and timed practice later. He points to Lynn Fuchs, David Purpura and Stanislas Dehaene as foundational, laments the split between qualitative and empirical researchers, and reminds readers that teachers must decide what research means in their own school.
points: The science of math draws on the same umbrella of learning science as the science of reading, but math lacks a single clear learning sequence, so the analogy is imperfect.
Math and reading are both cumulative, so a crack in early foundations such as linking numerals to quantities compromises later learning.
Thinking developmentally means treating young learners as novices, so explicit guidance and well-chosen materials beat minimally guided discovery.
Fact mastery should be built from understanding of operations to repeated practice and only then timed activities that consolidate facts in long-term memory.
Research tells educators what tends to work, but teachers must interpret it for their own school, and qualitative and empirical researchers need more cross-talk.
quotes: Both are highly cumulative, and early skills strongly predict later ones. If you cannot link letters to sounds, you will struggle to become a fluent reader.
There is a lot of research on how children learn about numbers and math. But in my experience, too little of it reaches teacher training and professional development.
Math lacks such a straightforward sequence. It is multifaceted, and the learning sequence for algebra differs from geometry.

Traditionalists tend to emphasize teaching the standard algorithm, while progressives usually argue that children should be taught multiple strategies and develop their own conceptual understanding. My take is that we should think about math instruction developmentally.

Kirschner also argued that minimally guided instructional approaches—like discovery learning and problem-based instruction—are less effective for most novices because those students don’t yet have enough knowledge stored in memory, so they need external guidance.
Once they’ve reached a high level of accuracy, timed activities help them consolidate their math facts into long-term memory, so they can retrieve them later when solving more advanced problems.

The science of math is meant to help teachers and school leaders become more effective at educating students. Researchers can tell you what tends to work. But teachers are the only ones who can figure out what that means in your school.
